overview: The Chagatai Khanate grew from the Central Asian lands and peoples assigned to Chagatai, a son of Chinggis Khan. Its history joined mobile courts, pasturelands and established towns from Transoxiana toward the Ili valley and Xinjiang. The atlas’s 1279 to 1530 interval covers several political phases. Its later outline wrongly stretches far into eastern Asia, beyond this khanate’s historical territories.

periods.title: An imperial inheritance
periods.summary: Chagatai’s territories belonged within the wider Mongol Empire.

periods.title: A regional khanate
periods.summary: Alghu brought civil administration under regional authority.

periods.title: Western and eastern division
periods.summary: Rival regional governments emerged during the fourteenth century.

periods.title: Timurid west and eastern khans
periods.summary: Timur dominated the west; eastern Chagatai rulers continued.

periods.title: Later eastern dynasties
periods.summary: Branches in eastern Turkestan survived beyond the atlas cutoff.

items.text: Chagatai’s inheritance included people and pasture, not just land within a neat border. At first, urban tax officials answered to the Great Khan. During the imperial civil wars of the 1260s, Alghu drew that administration under his own authority, making the regional khanate more independent.

Ergene Khatun governed as regent for her son Mubarak Shah during the 1250s. She negotiated amid struggles between Mongol princes and later married Alghu. Royal women could act as rulers and brokers of alliances; family relationships were central to political power, not merely background to it.

An agreement at Talas in 1269 called for princes to keep to seasonal pasturelands, keep their herds away from cultivated fields and leave town administration alone. These rules reveal a practical problem: grazing animals and growing crops could bring neighbours into conflict. An agreement records what leaders wanted, not guaranteed compliance.

Tarmashirin, whose reign Michal Biran dates to 1331 to 1334, was a Muslim ruler within a dynasty with varied religious histories. Other khans and commanders had converted earlier. His policies drew on existing Muslim networks; the population did not change its beliefs all at once when one ruler changed his.

From the 1340s, western and eastern governments increasingly followed separate paths. Powerful commanders dominated the west, where Timur became the effective ruler in 1370. Eastern Chagatai rulers retained power in Moghulistan. One dynasty’s name therefore appears across histories of several competing governments.

In 1221, before the separate khanate emerged, the traveller Chang Chun stayed in Almaliq’s fruit gardens. His account describes locally grown cotton made into thread, rope, cloth and padding. His party bought it for winter clothing. Cotton could look like wool, but no sheep needed shearing.

The same account describes farmers irrigating fields through canals and people carrying water in pitchers on their heads. Almaliq’s surroundings supported both orchards and pasture. Keeping a household supplied meant skilled cultivation, maintaining water channels and repeated carrying, rather than turning on a kitchen tap.

Kebek’s government issued silver dinars and dirhams in the early fourteenth century, and his name became associated with the money. Coinage helped connect the khan’s authority with everyday exchange. A small piece of silver could travel much farther than the person who first earned it.

A coin hoard found at Kultobe in Kazakhstan contained money from many mints, including Bukhara, Samarkand, Kashgar and Almaliq. The Azret Sultan Museum holds only a surviving transferred subset: 24 silver coins and two copper ones. Such finds connect a local hiding place with much wider networks of exchange.

Ibn Battuta’s account of his 1330s journey describes riverside pleasure gardens at Samarkand alongside damaged buildings. A traveller noticed both ruin and places to relax. His story adds a human glimpse of the city, though historians check his inconsistent chronology and other claims against independent evidence.

sections.title: Personal objects, disease and a queen’s monument

items.text: At Kara-Djigach in the Chüy valley, Qutluq Tärim was buried in 1338 or 1339 with a bracelet, a ring and a gold earring carrying four pearls. Archaeologists recorded these objects with her grave. They reveal personal adornment and access to valued materials, although one burial cannot tell us what every woman owned.

Researchers studying teeth from the same cemetery identified plague-bacterium DNA in three people buried during the 1338 to 1339 epidemic. Inscriptions also recorded an unusual surge of deaths. Combining documents, graves and ancient DNA identified a local health disaster and helped investigate its relationship to the later Black Death.

At Almaliq, Tughluq Temur’s tomb preserves impressive tilework and calligraphy. His widow Tini Khatun financed it, probably some years after his death in the fourteenth century. Its exact construction date is uncertain. A queen’s patronage helped turn mourning into a durable building that visitors can still study.

sections.title: Languages and short pieces of writing

items.text: A Christian gravestone for Sanmaq at Kara-Djigach includes the Syriac word “mawtānā”, meaning “pestilence”. This is the researchers’ Roman transcription of the inscription, dated around 1338. It preserves how a community described a terrible loss. The gravestone is distinct from the individuals whose teeth supplied the DNA evidence.

Chagatai also names an influential Turkic literary language. Its later classical literature flourished in Timurid centres such as Herat and Samarkand, and borrowed extensively from Persian and Arabic. Language history crossed political borders: a book called Chagatai was not necessarily written for a Chagatai khan.

A Samarkand silver coin from 1399 to 1400 reads “السلطان محمود خان”, or “Sultan Mahmud Khan”. It also names Timur. This later western example belongs to the era when Timur held real power while a khan supplied formal legitimacy. The Arabic lettering shows how two layers of authority could fit on one small coin.

ending.text: The khanate divided during the fourteenth century. Timur’s rise transformed western rule, while eastern Chagatai dynasties continued in Moghulistan and later Kashgar and Yarkand. Sultan Said established a new Kashgar-centred state in 1514; eastern branches lasted beyond 1530 into the seventeenth century. The atlas cutoff is not one conquest or the disappearance of Central Asia’s communities.
